docs.title: 1 - FLAreCAPTCHA
docs.text:
The challenge has a file named flarecaptcha.html, I opened it in a browser and started analyzing the source code.

I found this condition:

if (e.button === (Math.pow(5, 0) + Math.pow(1, 1)))

It is equivalent to:

if (e.button === 2)

So, we know that the code checks which mouse button was pressed.

I checked the MDN documentation and found that e.button === 2 means the right mouse button was pressed.

window.addEventListener('mouseup', (e) => {

if (e.button === 2) {

cancelHold();

}

});

This code calls cancelHold() when the right mouse button is released, I needed to hold the right mouse button for 2 seconds without releasing it.

After holding the button for 2 seconds, the page displays the flag.

docs.title: 2 - GhostStream
docs.text: We are given a file named GhostStream.wim, which uses the Windows Imaging Format (WIM).

docs.title: The mistake I made at first
docs.text:
The first thing I did was open it in HxD.

I found the magic bytes 4D 5A at offset 0xD0, so I removed the bytes before them and extracted the EXE file!

After analyzing the program, I found that it uses a file named PolyjuicePotion.txt. I created an empty file with that name and added values to its ADS. From the analysis, I figured out that it uses strings related to the movie Harry Potter. I may have guessed the right values, but the spelling was wrong, so I spent a lot of time on this challenge (._.)

docs.title: WIM file format
docs.text: We can use 7-Zip to extract the files. After extracting the contents, we get two files: GhostStream.exe and PolyjuicePotion.txt.

docs.title: Reversing the program
docs.text:
When analyzing the main function of GhostStream.exe, I found a pattern the program uses to import functions. It passes encoded data to the function at address 0000000140001130. I named this function loads_Processes.

After debugging, I found that ProcName changes to OpenClipboard. It is then passed to GetProcAddress and executed.

I traced this pattern in the other locations and gave those functions names, too.

When this function executes, copying and pasting no longer work, so it is better to NOP it.

It is also better to NOP the sleep function at address 0000000140002130.

I know these are simple things, but they may be useful for beginner REs.

At address 00000001400021E0, we can see an anti-debugging technique.

The value 0x11 stands for ThreadHideFromDebugger, so we should skip this call or NOP it while debugging. We can also use ScyllaHide.

Tip for beginner REs: If you find that an address in x64dbg does not match the address in IDA, load the file into PE-bear, go to Optional Header > DLL Characteristics, and change the value to 8120.

The function at address 0000000140001860 takes one argument: lpThreadParameter.

When analyzing and debugging this function, I found that only one block is important to us.

The value of dword_140006668 is hardcoded to 0. The challenge says, you aren't getting your nutrient paste until your debugger forces a confession out of it. So, we need to change its value to 1 or change jne to je to enter the if statement.

Now we know that the file has an alternate data stream (ADS).

We can extract it using this command:

more < PolyjuicePotion.txt:LordVoldemort

The value is AlbusDumbledore.

At LABEL_39, the program creates a pipe and connects to it.

Then, at address 0000000140001400, it loads a resource named Partner_CTF.exe. We can extract it using Resource Hacker, or find it in the temp directory after executing this function, because the program calls:

GetTempPathW(0x104u, Buffer);

Finally, it sends the buffer to the other program.

After execution, the program prints [*] The Polyjuice Potion is still effective, preventing the true identity from being revealed. This happens because it checks Buffer[0] against A. Our stream value is AlbusDumbledore, so the first character is A. If we change it to another character, this message will not appear. However, the message [FAILED] Try again with better debugging, which comes from Partner_CTF.exe, is still printed. Maybe we need to change the value to another character from the movie.

After more debugging and analysis, I found a function we had not analyzed yet: sub_140001B20. It contains a hint from the text in PolyjuicePotion.txt: 7 days.

While debugging, I found that WindowLongPtrW + 0x18 equals 0x2760, which is 10080 in decimal. This is the number of minutes in 7 days.

So, we need to move the instruction pointer past this block to skip it, then check whether the buffer changes to a word that does not start with A.

When we run until the WriteFile function, the value of Buffer is HarryPotter.

This may be the value the program expects. We can add it to the ADS with this command:

echo HarryPotter> PolyjuicePotion.txt:LordVoldemort

However, when I execute the program, it still prints [FAILED] Try again with better debugging. Maybe there is something else we need to edit in the other file.

docs.title: Reversing the Partner_CTF program
docs.text:
When analyzing Partner_CTF, I found that it creates a pipe connection to the other program and uses ReadFile to read the value from the buffer. Since we know the buffer value is HarryPotter, we can pass that value in the buffer and set NumberOfBytesRead (the value pointed to by the fourth argument, &NumberOfBytesRead) to 0xB to pass the debugger check.

In the following code, the program changes the memory permissions of strlen so that it can write shellcode to it, and then restores the permissions.

The string Str, which contains Bxs]bv`^u)TpcnolVjN, will be decoded into Piertotum Locomotor. However, Str_Variable, which contains Wingardium Leviosa, will be encoded.

We want the first string to be readable, but not the second one, so we only need to execute this function on the first string.

Further down, the return value of strlen for the second string is compared.

So, it should return the actual length of Wingardium Leviosa, which is 0x12.

Now, set a breakpoint at address 000000014000167B, where the flag is checked.

docs.title: My initial analysis
docs.text:
When I looked at the strings in the file, I thought it statically used the OpenSSL library. I also found many constants from different encryption algorithms. When I used the Findcrypt plugin, it showed many indicators of encryption algorithms, but the functions using these constants still needed to be renamed.

So, I tried IDA FLIRT. The strings showed that the program uses OpenSSL 1.0.1e (11 Feb 2013), so I downloaded it and created a signature file. I followed the instructions in this article, then went to View → Subviews → Signatures and added the signature. It identified only 67 functions.

You can learn more about FLIRT in The IDA Pro Book, Chapter 12.

Then I thought that, since the binary had many functions similar to or implementing the same functionality as the OpenSSL library, I could write a Python script to compare the program with a compiled version of OpenSSL, such as a DLL.

I found a tool named Diaphora and used it to compare the two files. It reported more than 35% similarity. The analysis had not finished yet, but the tool crashed.

I tried another approach. I went to the main function and found an important string: "BTC donation address: 1FhDPLPpw18X4srecguG3MxJYe4a1JsZnd (tpruvot)\n\n".

I searched for this string and found that the program uses source code from CPUMiner-Multi. I compared our program with cpu-miner.c and found that they were very similar. Then I started analyzing our decompiled code alongside this source code.

I also downloaded and compiled the project. Then I compared the important and interesting functions.

It is very similar to our program, and now I can name the functions.

In the main function, our program sets some constants that force it to run in benchmark mode and use the algorithm where opt_algo = 39:

opt_benchmark = 1;
opt_algo = 39;

The function miner_thread at address 0000000140100920 is very similar to the source code. The important part for us is switch ( opt_algo ) at address 00000001401012B0. It jumps to the case for the selected algorithm. In our program, opt_algo is set to 39 in the main function.

In the source code, value 39 corresponds to ALGO_SHA256D. The program then calls scanhash_sha256d at address 0000000140134F70 in our binary.

This function contains an important detail that is not present in the other functions or the source code. It calls GetVolumeInformationA, which retrieves our machine's volume serial number and stores it in VolumeSerialNumber.

Then it checks whether the length of rpc_user is 64. We need to use the --user option and pass a 64-character string. This check is important because it sets v9 to 1.

For example, I entered:

ToxicMiner.exe --user=11223344556677889900aabbccddeeff11223344556677889900aabbccddeeff

It stores every two hex digits as one byte.

After this loop, Buf2 contains the value of rpc_user as bytes.

At address 0000000140135156, this value is compared with Buf1.

Then it runs the same function on Buf1 and stores the result in v29.

It then compares this result with Buf2, which contains rpc_user as bytes.

So, we need to know two values to enter this loop: rpc_user and VolumeSerialNumber.

However, after memcmp, there is a block of code that does not depend on rpc_user. This is because sub_140134CA0 does not depend on the value of Buf2; it overwrites Buf2 and eventually returns the value stored there.

After the memcmp instruction, the program seems to perform the operations needed to get the flag. unk_1401BD3B0 contains encrypted data, which may be the encrypted flag. At the end, the program prints Accepted:.

So, we need to brute-force VolumeSerialNumber. It is 4 bytes long, which means there are 2^32 possible values, from 0 to 0xFFFFFFFF.

I heard about a technology that lets threads run on the GPU instead of the CPU, which could make our script much faster. It is called CUDA. I'll try it later, but for now I'll use OpenMP. It runs on the CPU and supports cross-platform, shared-memory parallel programming in C, C++, and Fortran.

docs.title: Solver
docs.text:
When I first solved this challenge, I had trouble writing code that exactly matched sub_140134CA0, so I loaded the program itself and called this function directly.

Script:

#include <windows.h>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>

uint8_t encrypted_flag[51] = {
    0xF4,0xF9,0x65,0x9F,0x31,0xF3,0xDA,0x5C,0xF1,0x37,0xA1,0xB8,0xCF,0x90,0xA1,0x58,
    0x1E,0xEB,0xE4,0x99,0xA7,0xC1,0x1B,0x15,0x02,0xAF,0x74,0x63,0xD3,0xB2,0x19,0x28,
    0x66,0xDE,0x3D,0xE9,0x71,0x63,0xE7,0x75,0xDF,0xE4,0xAB,0x61,0x6F,0xB9,0x0C,0x27,
    0x89,0xFC,0x87
};

using DeriveKey = uint64_t(__fastcall*)(uint32_t, uint32_t, uint8_t*);

std::atomic<bool> found{false};
uint32_t foundSerial;
char flag[52];

void rc4(uint8_t* key, const uint8_t* data, uint8_t* out, int len) {
    uint8_t s[256];
    for (int i = 0; i < 256; i++) s[i] = i;

    int j = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 256; i++) {
        j = (j + s[i] + key[i % 16]) & 255;
        uint8_t t = s[i];
        s[i] = s[j];
        s[j] = t;
    }

    int i = 0;
    j = 0;

    for (int k = 0; k < len; k++) {
        i = (i + 1) & 255;
        j = (j + s[i]) & 255;

        uint8_t t = s[i];
        s[i] = s[j];
        s[j] = t;

        out[k] = data[k] ^ s[(s[i] + s[j]) & 255];
    }
}

int main() {
    HMODULE mod = LoadLibraryExA(
        "ToxicMiner.exe", nullptr, DONT_RESOLVE_DLL_REFERENCES
    );

    if (!mod) {
        puts("Failed to load ToxicMiner.exe");
        return 1;
    }

    DWORD oldProtect;
    VirtualProtect(mod, 0x200000, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, &oldProtect);

    auto derive = reinterpret_cast<DeriveKey>(
        reinterpret_cast<uint8_t*>(mod) + 0x134CA0
    );

    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    #pragma omp parallel for schedule(dynamic, 65536)
    for (int64_t n = 0; n <= 0xFFFFFFFFLL; n++) {
        if (found.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) continue;

        uint8_t key[32], plain[51];
        derive((uint32_t)n, 189800062, key);
        rc4(key, encrypted_flag, plain, 51);

        if (memcmp(plain + 38, "@flare-on.com", 13) == 0) {
            bool expected = false;

            if (found.compare_exchange_strong(expected, true)) {
                foundSerial = (uint32_t)n;
                memcpy(flag, plain, 51);
                flag[51] = '\0';
            }
        }
    }

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    if (found) {
        printf("Serial: 0x%08X\n", foundSerial);
        printf("Flag: %s\n", flag);
    } else {
        puts("Flag not found");
    }

    printf("Time: %.2f sec\n",
        std::chrono::duration<double>(end - start).count());

    return 0;
}

Compile and run: 1. Open x64 Native Tools Command Prompt for VS 2022. 2. Compile the code:

cl /O2 /openmp solver.cpp
  1. Run it:
solver.exe

docs.title: Initial Network Analysis
docs.text:
The program establishes a network connection and exchanges encrypted data. To inspect the traffic, I first needed to identify the encryption algorithm and determine how to decrypt the payloads.

I used FakeNet-NG to respond to the program's requests.

The binary is written in Rust and is stripped, making static analysis more difficult. I therefore traced the network APIs used to send and receive data.

When execution reached the send function, the RDX register pointed to the following HTTP request:

POST /exfil HTTP/1.1
Host: 192.168.56.102:8080
User-Agent: ureq/2.12.1
Accept: */*
accept-encoding: gzip
Content-Length: 264

When the breakpoint was hit again, the program sent the encrypted request body. Its contents were similar to the corresponding data in the PCAP, but one byte differed.

Execution then reached recv. The response differed because FakeNet-NG did not return the response data expected by the program.

I therefore created a custom HTTP server, using this script as a starting point.

The PCAP shows that the program connects to 192.168.56.102:8080. To let a local server receive traffic addressed to that IP, I assigned the address to the Ethernet0 interface with the following command:

netsh interface ipv4 add address name="Ethernet0" address=192.168.56.102 mask=255.255.255.0

To remove the address after testing, run:

netsh interface ipv4 delete address name="Ethernet0" address=192.168.56.102

For more information about netsh and interface addresses, see this explanation.

The PCAP contains six TCP streams. I extracted the request Content-Length values and corresponding response bodies, then added them to the custom server script.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
based on https://gist.github.com/mdonkers/63e115cc0c79b4f6b8b3a6b797e485c7
Usage::
    ./server.py [<port>]

"""
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
import hashlib
import logging
import os
import threading


PORT = 8080
SAVE_DIR = "loot"            # every request body is saved here (binary-safe)

# Make the response look like the original server
PROTOCOL = "HTTP/1.0"         # 'HTTP/1.0' -> connection closes after the reply
SERVER_VERSION = "BaseHTTP/0.6"
SYS_VERSION = "Python/3.8.10"  # together: "Server: BaseHTTP/0.6 Python/3.8.10"
SEND_CONTENT_TYPE = None      # e.g. "text/html"; None = don't send the header
EXTRA_HEADERS = {}            # e.g. {"Content-Length": "36", "X-Foo": "bar"}

# Recorded responses from the pcap: (request Content-Length, response body as hex)
RESPONSES = [
    (264,     "8412fb4003efeaf701c2487f68c47edb1fc630c1e049ffccd27f72add78e3e652d0ec7e5"),
    (3121086, "8412fb4003efeaf701c2487f68c47edb1fc630c1e049ffc4d16069b7c69d3370774addf2e3"),
    (2736058, "8412fb4003efeaf701c2487f68c47edb1fc630c1e049ffdcda7b7cb1cc9b38747107d6f6aaa89ab9"),
    (3061432, "8412fb4003efeaf701c2487f68c47edb1fc630c1e049ffc6de7b7ebed78c31652d0ec7e5"),
    (3079606, "8412fb4003efeaf701c2487f68c47edb1fc630c1e049ffc8c6697ca9cc9d39656607d6f6aaa89ab9"),
    (2842789, ""),            # last reply had headers only (empty body)
]


def choose_response(method, path, body, n, headers):
    """Return the bytes to send back.  <- the one function to rewrite per challenge.

    method  : "GET" / "POST" / ...
    path    : e.g. "/exfil"
    body    : request body (bytes)
    n       : request number, starting at 1
    headers : request headers (headers.get("User-Agent") ...)
    """
    # 1) match by request size (works even if requests arrive out of order)
    for length, hex_body in RESPONSES:
        if len(body) == length:
            return bytes.fromhex(hex_body)
    # 2) fallback: by order, repeating the last one
    return bytes.fromhex(RESPONSES[min(n, len(RESPONSES)) - 1][1])
# ===================================================================

_lock = threading.Lock()
_count = 0


def hexdump(data, n=64):
    return " ".join(f"{b:02x}" for b in data[:n]) + (" ..." if len(data) > n else "")


class S(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    protocol_version = PROTOCOL
    server_version = SERVER_VERSION
    sys_version = SYS_VERSION

    def _set_response(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        if SEND_CONTENT_TYPE:
            self.send_header('Content-type', SEND_CONTENT_TYPE)
        for k, v in EXTRA_HEADERS.items():
            self.send_header(k, v)
        self.end_headers()

    def _read_body(self):
        # read in chunks: big bodies (MBs) can't be read reliably in one call
        remaining = int(self.headers.get('Content-Length') or 0)
        data = b''
        while remaining > 0:
            chunk = self.rfile.read(min(65536, remaining))
            if not chunk:
                logging.warning("client closed early, %d bytes missing", remaining)
                break
            data += chunk
            remaining -= len(chunk)
        return data

    def _handle(self, method):
        global _count
        post_data = self._read_body()
        with _lock:
            _count += 1
            n = _count

        # binary-safe logging (no .decode('utf-8'), it crashes on binary data)
        logging.info("%s request #%d,\nPath: %s\nHeaders:\n%s\n\nBody: %d bytes, sha256=%s\nHead: %s\n",
                     method, n, str(self.path), str(self.headers), len(post_data),
                     hashlib.sha256(post_data).hexdigest(), hexdump(post_data))
        if post_data:
            os.makedirs(SAVE_DIR, exist_ok=True)
            with open(os.path.join(SAVE_DIR, f"req_{n:02d}_{len(post_data)}.bin"), "wb") as f:
                f.write(post_data)

        resp = choose_response(method, self.path, post_data, n, self.headers)
        logging.info("-> replying with %d bytes: %s\n", len(resp), hexdump(resp))
        self._set_response()
        if resp:
            self.wfile.write(resp)

    def do_GET(self):
        self._handle("GET")

    def do_POST(self):
        self._handle("POST")

    def do_PUT(self):
        self._handle("PUT")


def run(server_class=ThreadingHTTPServer, handler_class=S, port=PORT):
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    server_address = ('', port)
    httpd = server_class(server_address, handler_class)
    logging.info('Starting httpd...\n')
    try:
        httpd.serve_forever()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    httpd.server_close()
    logging.info('Stopping httpd...\n')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    from sys import argv

    if len(argv) == 2:
        run(port=int(argv[1]))
    else:
        run()

docs.title: Recovering the RC4 Key and File Paths
docs.text:
By tracing the call stack for send, I found a call at 0000000140003E1E inside the function at 00000001400029AA. This function is referenced from main, so I analyzed it next.

At 00000001400034DB, I found an XOR operation that produces the string i11_b3_p1und3r1n_y3r_d474. The program later uses this string as the RC4 key.

The functions at 1400052E2 and 140005281 implement the RC4 Key Scheduling Algorithm (KSA) and Pseudo-Random Generation Algorithm (PRGA), respectively.

The same RC4 functions are used again at 00000001400041F0. In this case, the data referenced by v301.m128i_i64[1] becomes C:\Users\flare\Desktop\important.jpg after the RC4 operation. This indicates that the operation is decrypting the server response.

I created the following file to continue tracing this function:

To find where the encrypted response data came from, I traced the indirect call (*(v200 + 48))(v199, &v301), located at 140079F5C.

While stepping through this function, execution hit my breakpoint on recv. At that point, v301.m128i_i64[1] held the address of the encrypted response data returned by the server.

The buffer was located at 0x4A7210.

After RC4_PRGA executed, the response decrypted to C:\Users\flare\Desktop\important.jpg.

Decrypting all response bodies with RC4 in CyberChef produced the following file paths:

C:\Users\flare\Desktop\important.jpg
C:\Users\flare\Desktop\anothercat.jpg
C:\Users\flare\Desktop\yetanothercat.jpg
C:\Users\flare\Desktop\catcatcat.jpg
C:\Users\flare\Desktop\myfavoritecat.jpg

docs.title: Tracing File Reads and Huffman Compression
docs.text:
This showed that v301.m128i_i64[1] points to the response data containing encrypted file paths. Next, I needed to trace how the program reads and processes the file contents.

To trace file processing, I replaced the contents of the files with test and set breakpoints on kernel32.dll!CreateFileW and ntdll.dll!NtReadFile.

ntdll.dll!NtReadFile read the contents (test). I then set a hardware breakpoint on access to this buffer.

The buffer was accessed at 0000000140002AB0 and then passed to sub_1400016B6. Its operations and constants resemble SipHash; I compared the implementation with this reference implementation.

The functions computes a hash for the byte being processed. The operations and constants in sub_1400016B6 resemble SipHash. I compared the implementation with the reference source code.

While debugging, I found that the file contents pass through a Huffman compression pipeline. I used this reference implementation to identify the corresponding stages in the binary. At this point, I had identified the main blocks but had not yet analyzed every stage in detail.

After Huffman compression, the resulting message is encrypted with RC4 using the same key, i11_b3_p1und3r1n_y3r_d474.

I decrypted the captured data with RC4 and recovered the data that existed before encryption. However, my first attempt to decode it with the reference Huffman decoder did not reproduce the original file. This did not prove that the Huffman algorithm itself was modified, so I investigated the message format, header, and bit-packing logic to identify the difference.

Using the reference source code, I identified six functions or stages to look for in the binary so I could understand the encoder and implement a compatible decoder:

getFrequency()
createHuffmanTree()
getCodeLength()
generateCanonicalCode()
writeHeader()
writeEncodedText()

docs.title: Analyzing the Huffman Compression Pipeline
docs.text:
First, I identified the block corresponding to getFrequency(), which starts at 0000000140002AA7. It counts the occurrences of each byte in the input data.

Next, I identified the block corresponding to createHuffmanTree(), which starts at 0000000140002CF8. It repeatedly removes the two lowest-frequency nodes, combines them into a parent node, and inserts the parent back into the heap.

The function at 00000001400053AB corresponds to getCodeLength(). It traverses the Huffman tree, tracks the depth of each node, and stores the depth of each leaf in a symbol-indexed code-length table.

Next, I examined the block corresponding to generateCanonicalCode(). It collects symbols with non-zero code lengths, sorts the entries, and generates canonical codes from their lengths.

I then examined the block corresponding to writeEncodedText(). It reads each input byte, looks up its Huffman code, and appends the code to a bit buffer.

After encoding the input, the program packs the Huffman bitstream into bytes.

docs.title: Analyzing writeHeader()
docs.text:
Finally, I examined the block corresponding to writeHeader(). I needed to understand how the header and compressed payload are serialized so I could implement a compatible decoder.

I first analyzed the helper function sub_1400053FE.

The function sub_1400053FE extracts bits from an integer and appends their ASCII representations ('0' or '1') to a buffer. I verified this behavior in the debugger by passing the value 0x100 with a bit width of 0xB (11 bits). The buffer then contained 00100000000, confirming that the integer is represented using the requested 11-bit width.

The next call, sub_1400053FE(&DataBitString, lengthOfCompData, 0x20u), appends the compressed-data length using 32 bits. In this test, lengthOfCompData was 1, so the appended field was the 32-bit representation of 1 (31 zero bits followed by one). The function appends this field to the existing buffer; it does not return the bit string itself. Note that the width is 32 bits, not 32 bytes.

I then examined sub_140005457. It iterates over a byte array and calls sub_1400053FE for each byte with a bit width of eight. Therefore, each source byte is appended to the buffer as eight ASCII bit characters. The third argument specifies how many bytes to process.

Using these observations, I analyzed the four calls that construct the serialized message. The program appends the code-length table size using 11 bits, then the compressed-data length using 32 bits. It next appends the code-length table and the compressed payload, with each byte represented by eight ASCII bit characters.

The program then packs the complete serialized bit string into bytes. This is a separate packing stage from the earlier loop, which packs only the Huffman payload.

docs.title: Validating the Decoder and Locating the HTTP Payload
docs.text:
After the RC4 function executes, the message is encrypted. To determine where the resulting buffer is used, I set a hardware breakpoint on the buffer and traced its subsequent accesses.

I used a test file containing test to validate the process. To recover the original content, I reversed the encoding steps:

Encrypted HTTP body
    -> RC4 decryption
    -> Parse the Huffman container
    -> Huffman decoding
    -> Original file bytes

The data recovered after RC4 decryption matched the serialized Huffman data observed in the debugger before encryption.

I then wrote a Huffman decoder for the recovered container format. The decoder first converts the message into a bit string while preserving leading zeros. It reads the 11-bit table-length field and the following 32-bit compressed-data length, then extracts the code-length table and compressed payload using those lengths. Because the fields are not byte-aligned, the offsets are calculated in bits rather than by slicing the original byte array.

Next, the decoder sorts the symbols by code length and symbol value, then reconstructs the canonical Huffman codes. It uses the reconstructed codes to map the compressed bitstream back to the original bytes.

data = bytes.fromhex("")

def huffman_decode(data):
    bits = bin(int.from_bytes(data, "big"))[2:].zfill(len(data) * 8)
    if len(bits) < 43:
        raise ValueError("not a Huffman container")
    table_len, n_bytes = int(bits[:11], 2), int(bits[11:43], 2)
    if table_len != 256:
        raise ValueError("not a Catthief Huffman container")
    pos = 43
    lengths = [int(bits[pos + 8*i:pos + 8*i + 8], 2) for i in range(table_len)]
    pos += 8 * table_len
    body = bits[pos:pos + 8 * n_bytes]
    if len(body) != 8 * n_bytes:
        raise ValueError("incomplete Huffman data")
    entries = sorted((length, sym) for sym, length in enumerate(lengths) if length)
    if not entries:
        raise ValueError("empty Huffman table")
    max_len = max(length for length, _ in entries)
    lookup = [None] * (1 << max_len)
    code = prev = 0
    for length, sym in entries:
        code <<= length - prev
        base = code << (max_len - length)
        for k in range(1 << (max_len - length)):
            lookup[base + k] = (sym, length)
        code += 1; prev = length
    body += "0" * max_len
    out = bytearray(); i = 0
    while i < 8 * n_bytes:
        hit = lookup[int(body[i:i + max_len], 2)]
        if hit is None:
            break
        out.append(hit[0]); i += hit[1]
    return bytes(out)

if __name__ == "__main__":

    print(huffman_decode(data))

#!/usr/bin/env python3

from pathlib import Path
import sys

KEY = b'i11_b3_p1und3r1n_y3r_d474'


def rc4(key, data):
    s = list(range(256)); j = 0
    for i in range(256):
        j = (j + s[i] + key[i % len(key)]) & 255
        s[i], s[j] = s[j], s[i]
    out = bytearray(len(data)); i = j = 0
    for n, b in enumerate(data):
        i = (i + 1) & 255; j = (j + s[i]) & 255
        s[i], s[j] = s[j], s[i]
        out[n] = b ^ s[(s[i] + s[j]) & 255]
    return bytes(out)


def huffman_decode(data):
    bits = bin(int.from_bytes(data, "big"))[2:].zfill(len(data) * 8)
    if len(bits) < 43:
        raise ValueError("not a Huffman container")
    table_len, n_bytes = int(bits[:11], 2), int(bits[11:43], 2)
    if table_len != 256:
        raise ValueError("not a Catthief Huffman container")
    pos = 43
    lengths = [int(bits[pos + 8*i:pos + 8*i + 8], 2) for i in range(table_len)]
    pos += 8 * table_len
    body = bits[pos:pos + 8 * n_bytes]
    if len(body) != 8 * n_bytes:
        raise ValueError("incomplete Huffman data")
    entries = sorted((length, sym) for sym, length in enumerate(lengths) if length)
    if not entries:
        raise ValueError("empty Huffman table")
    max_len = max(length for length, _ in entries)
    lookup = [None] * (1 << max_len)
    code = prev = 0
    for length, sym in entries:
        code <<= length - prev
        base = code << (max_len - length)
        for k in range(1 << (max_len - length)):
            lookup[base + k] = (sym, length)
        code += 1; prev = length
    body += "0" * max_len
    out = bytearray(); i = 0
    while i < 8 * n_bytes:
        hit = lookup[int(body[i:i + max_len], 2)]
        if hit is None:
            break
        out.append(hit[0]); i += hit[1]
    return bytes(out)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print(f"Usage: {Path(sys.argv[0]).name} <objects-folder>")
        return 2
    src_root = Path(sys.argv[1]).expanduser().resolve()
    if not src_root.is_dir():
        print(f"Not a folder: {src_root}", file=sys.stderr); return 2
    dst_root = src_root.with_name(src_root.name + "_decoded")
    files = sorted(p for p in src_root.rglob("*") if p.is_file())
    for src in files:
        try:
            plain = rc4(KEY, src.read_bytes())
            try:
                result = huffman_decode(plain)
                mode = "RC4 + Huffman"
            except ValueError:
                result, mode = plain, "RC4 only"
            if result.startswith(b"\xff\xd8") and b"\xff\xd9" in result:
                result = result[:result.rfind(b"\xff\xd9") + 2]
            dst = dst_root / src.relative_to(src_root).parent / f"{src.stem}_decoded{src.suffix}"
            dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); dst.write_bytes(result)
            print(f"[{mode}] {src.relative_to(src_root)} -> {dst.relative_to(dst_root)}")
        except OSError as e:
            print(f"[FAIL] {src}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
    print(f"Output: {dst_root}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

I changed their file extensions to .jfif and opened them in an image viewer. I found the flag in one of the images: exfil(8)_decoded.jpeg.

docs.title: Analyzing a Single Node
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>

typedef struct Node
{
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

int main()
{
    Node node;

    node.value = 10;
    node.next = NULL;

    return 0;
}

The assembly does not clearly indicate that a structure is being used. The compiler simply writes values to memory, just as it would for ordinary local variables.

One small clue is that the second member begins at [rbp+10h] instead of [rbp+0Ch]. This is because the compiler inserted four bytes of padding after the int member so that the pointer is aligned on an 8-byte boundary.

However, this alone is not enough to conclude that the object is a linked list—or even a structure. From the assembly alone, we only know that there is a 4-byte value followed by an 8-byte value.

We can't identify a linked list from a single instruction or a single object. Instead, we recognize the overall pattern created by pointer dereferences, traversal loops, and NULL termination. We will see these patterns in the following examples.

When the program is compiled with debug information (PDB), ida can recover the structure definition and display the member names and offsets.

docs.title: Recursive Functions in Assembly (x64dbg)
docs.text: I wrote two simple programs in c, compiled them, and traced their execution in x64dbg to understand how recursive functions works in assembly.

docs.title: Recursive Functions Without a Return Value (void)
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>

void func(int n)
{
    if (n == 0)
        return;

    printf("%d\n", n);

    func(n - 1);
}

int main()
{
    func(3);
}

The function prints the current value of n, decrements it by one, and recursively calls itself until n becomes zero. Since the function's return type is void, it does not return a value to its caller.

The main function calls the func and sends to it the value 3

after the call instruction, the caller does not use the value in eax. Although eax may contain a value left by previous instructions or function calls, the caller ignores it because a void function does not return a meaningful value.

When a function calls another function, the CPU pushes the return address onto the stack and creates a new stack frame for the callee.

The same behavior occurs when a function calls itself recursively. Every recursive call creates its own independent stack frame and stores its own return address on the stack.

Once the base case is reached, the recursive calls begin to return. Each ret instruction pops the corresponding return address from the stack and transfers execution back to the instruction immediately following the call instruction in the previous stack frame. This process continues until all recursive calls have returned.

docs.title: Recursive Functions With a Return Value
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>

int func(int n)
{
    if (n == 0)
        return 1;

    return n * func(n - 1);
}

int main()
{
    printf("%d\n", func(3));

    return 0;
}

The function recursively calls itself until it reaches the base case (n == 0), where it returns 1.

Once the base case is reached, the recursive calls stop. The program then begins stack unwinding. Each ret instruction returns execution to the instruction immediately following the corresponding call.

In this example, execution returns to address 0x00007FF613F218CE. At this point, the caller uses the return value from the previous recursive call to compute its own return value. This process repeats until all recursive calls have returned.

The return value of each recursive call is stored in rax. The caller then uses this value to perform the multiplication before returning to its caller.
